items.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem ...
items.excerpt: Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem featuring interconnected phishing kit operators (Storm-2990) and an illicit marketplace (Storm-3119) selling tools for large-scale phishing. Collaborating with global law enforcement, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit facilitated a major disruption of this infrastructure, offering critical insights for defenders monitoring underground tool distribution and phishing-as-a-service networks.

items.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target ...
items.excerpt: Threat actors launched a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign exploiting Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. By disguising malicious emails as legitimate outage alerts, attackers targeted organizations across multiple sectors. Infrastructure defenders should monitor for spoofed service-status domains and reinforce email authentication controls to mitigate this widespread credential-harvesting tactic.

items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: Microsoft researchers dissect the EvilTokens campaign, revealing the underlying mechanics of device code phishing that bypasses traditional credential theft. The analysis provides technical indicators, attacker infrastructure details, and defensive recommendations. Infrastructure teams should implement strict OAuth consent policies, monitor for suspicious device code approvals, and deploy token lifecycle management controls.

items.title: Inside an AI‑enabled device code phishing campaign | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: This analysis details a sophisticated phishing campaign leveraging artificial intelligence to automate and personalize device code requests. By bypassing traditional password theft, attackers directly target OAuth authorization flows. Defenders must review conditional access policies, monitor for anomalous device code approvals, and deploy AI-aware detection rules to counter this evolving identity threat.

items.title: Crafty Microsoft Teams Booking Flow Disguises Device Code Phishing | Huntress
items.excerpt: Huntress researchers uncover a novel phishing technique that disguises device code requests within legitimate-looking Microsoft Teams booking flows. This tactic exploits user trust in familiar collaboration tools to bypass security awareness. Infrastructure defenders should monitor Teams API abuse, validate booking flow integrations, and educate users on recognizing disguised authorization prompts.

items.title: Microsoft 365 device code phishing campaign bypasses password stealing | RL Blog
items.excerpt: ReversingLabs details a widespread Microsoft 365 phishing campaign that sidesteps password harvesting by exploiting device code authorization flows. The article provides actionable detection rules, infrastructure indicators, and configuration hardening steps. Defenders should audit M365 consent policies, restrict device code usage to approved applications, and enhance monitoring for anomalous authentication patterns.

items.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover | Proofpoint US
items.excerpt: Proofpoint examines how device code phishing has evolved into a primary method for identity takeover, circumventing multi-factor authentication and password-based defenses. The report outlines attacker tactics, infrastructure patterns, and mitigation strategies. IT defenders should prioritize monitoring OAuth consent grants and implementing device code approval workflows to secure enterprise identity perimeters.

items.title: CVE-2026-130235
items.excerpt: In the Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library, outbound HTTP requests are not restricted to the configured Okta organization domain when processing certain URL formats. If a URL parameter is modified to specify an external host, the library may transmit the configured SSWS API token to that unintended destination.

items.title: CVE-2026-133659
items.excerpt:
Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account

items.title: CVE-2026-115342
items.excerpt: Argument injection in OpenVPN version 2.4.0 through 2.6.23 and 2.7_alpha1 through 2.7.8 on Windows allows local authenticated users to bypass interactive service option validation and add arbitrary configuration options via a crafted command line.

items.title: CVE-2026-130151
items.excerpt: Okta Privileged Access (OPA) Gateway includes a version of the FreeRDP library affected by memory management issues in its smartcard redirection handling. When an RDP session is established meeting specific session criteria, command execution within the context of the local Gateway service account may be allowed.

items.title: CVE-2026-130179
items.excerpt: The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library systematically writes per-request authentication credentials to a shared HTTP client instance, rather than being isolated to individual outbound request objects. When using scoped child clients, a subsequent scoped request can overwrite the shared client configuration. Because the original parent client credential has not been restored, subsequent outbound requests may be transmitted using the newly written credential, which can result in subsequent actions

items.title: CVE-2026-130236
items.excerpt: In the Auth0 Authorization Extension, request authentication handling can process claims from query parameters independently of header validation. Under specific preconditions, this may allow an authenticated tenant user to issue requests to the extension's administrative endpoints. Also, input handling during rule generation may permit modification of the tenant login rule published by the extension.

items.title: CVE-2026-130234
items.excerpt: The Okta Swift Management SDK does not percent-encode forward slash (/) characters during path parameter interpolation. If an application supplies input containing relative path sequences (e.g., ../) to an SDK method, standard URL normalization may direct the outbound request to an alternative Okta Management API endpoint.
